summary: This informational memo discusses how the analog nature of optical networking affects GMPLS control. Physical impairments in the optical layer can limit which paths are usable, so the document describes constraints that routing and signalling protocols may need to take into account.

plainLanguage.summary: Light travelling through fibre weakens and distorts, so not every route between two points can carry every signal. RFC 4054 lists the physical effects that limit optical routes, shows with worked numbers how they cap distance and speed, and describes what a GMPLS control plane would have to know to choose routes that survive both the physics and fibre cuts.

subtitle: How the physics of light limits which routes an optical network can actually take.

tldr.problem: Optical networks carry signals as analog light, so signal quality falls with distance and with every amplifier and optical element on the path. A routing protocol that ignores this can pick paths that will not work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys the main constraints, such as polarization mode dispersion and amplifier noise, works out example distance and span limits from them, and names the link information a GMPLS routing process would need for each approach.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational survey: it defines no protocol, but sets out the choices an operator has, from pre-qualified path tables to explicit per-link impairment state, plus shared-risk groups for physical diversity.

today: RFC 4054 is an Informational RFC from May 2005 that surveys constraints on optical layer routing for GMPLS. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Optical Routing Is Harder
sections.content:
Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) aims to extend label switching to transport networks, including optical networks built from optical cross-connects, transponders and optical add-drop multiplexers. RFC 4054 surveys the aspects of optical networking that make routing there harder than in packet networks.

The core difference: optical technology is analog, not digital, and the optical layer sits at the bottom of the transport hierarchy, so it is tied to the physical geography of the network. The RFC groups the challenges into four: constraints from software-reconfigurable network elements, constraints inside a single all-optical domain with no wavelength conversion, complications in networks that mix all-optical and opaque architectures, and the impact of diversity constraints, meaning the need to keep backup paths physically separate.

The document is a requirements survey for the IPO working group. It deliberately does not discuss alternative ways of controlling an optical network, only what routing must cope with under GMPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Choosing a route for light is not like choosing a route for packets: the signal itself degrades with distance, and the fibre follows real geography. This document lists what a GMPLS routing process must take into account.

sections.title: Reconfigurable Network Elements
sections.content:
Control-plane design usually assumes the only software-reconfigurable element is the optical layer cross-connect (OLXC). The RFC points to others on the horizon: tunable lasers and receivers, and reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexers (OADMs). Inside such a system, adaptation functions at the subnetwork edge map incoming short-reach optical channels onto the long-reach wavelength or wavelength group that will cross the all-optical subnetwork.

Adaptation affects routing in several ways. Multiplexing, electrical or optical time-division, combines input channels onto one wavelength, and the combined signal must then be routed as a group. Adaptation grouping manages sets of wavelengths, for example groups of four, that must be added or dropped together. Laser tunability ranges from fixed frequency to tuning across the whole dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) band, at varying speeds.

Connectivity between adaptation functions is limited too: multiplexed or grouped channels must travel together, only functions with mutually tunable lasers or receivers can connect, and the OADM switching itself may forbid dropping some wavelengths, tie dropped wavelengths to fixed ports, or cap how many groupings one OADM can drop. Retuning a laser or dropping another grouping changes the port-to-port connectivity, and that connectivity change may also change Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) relationships. GMPLS can either treat connectivity as set outside it, detecting and advertising changes made by vendor element management systems, or try to control it directly, which would mean voluminous, vendor-specific state.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical boxes increasingly let software retune lasers and reconfigure add-drop multiplexers, which changes which ports can talk to which. A routing protocol must either track those changes or hand control of them to the vendor's management system.

sections.title: Impairments in a Single All-Optical Domain
sections.content:
Older optical networks were opaque: transponders converted every link to electrical and back, regenerating the signal with retiming and reshaping, so bit rate and frame format did not matter end to end. Those transponders are expensive, so operators build domains of transparency, all-optical subnetworks larger than one transport system. The RFC assumes a domain too large to guarantee adequate signal quality on every route, and asks which impairments routing must then handle.

Impairments are linear or nonlinear. Linear effects, independent of signal power and acting on each wavelength alone, include polarization mode dispersion (PMD), amplifier spontaneous emission (ASE) and chromatic dispersion; nonlinearities also cause crosstalk between channels. Which ones routing must treat explicitly depends on vendor design, fibre characteristics, service speeds, network size and the operator's engineering strategy.

PMD splits a signal into two polarizations that arrive at slightly different times. The requirement is that the time-average differential group delay stay below a fraction of the bit duration; a typical value for the fraction is 10%. For older fibre with a PMD parameter of 0.5 picoseconds per square root of kilometre, that caps a transparent segment at 400 km at 10 Gb/s and 25 km at 40 Gb/s. Newer fibre at 0.1 picoseconds per square root of kilometre raises those limits to 10000 km and 625 km. The only link-specific number routing needs is link-PMD-square, the sum of the span values along the link.

ASE is noise added by optical amplifiers, which erodes the optical signal-to-noise ratio the receiver needs. In the RFC's worked example, with a launch power of 4 dBm, a required ratio of 20 dB with forward error correction, a 12.5 GHz bandwidth and 25 dB amplifier gain, a path can span at most 10 amplifiers; drop forward error correction and raise the requirement to 25 dB, and the limit falls to 3. Current systems are often limited to 6 spans of 80 km. Routing needs only link-noise, the sum of the span noise on the link, and the rule that total noise stay below launch power divided by the minimum acceptable ratio.

Other impairments the RFC treats as boundable by system engineering rather than routing state: polarization dependent loss, chromatic dispersion with its residual after compensation, crosstalk between channels, and the narrowing of the effective passband as filters cascade. Nonlinearities, it says, are unlikely to be tractable in a routing algorithm at all, because they couple routes together and depend on detailed plant knowledge; a fixed margin of 1 or 2 dB in the required signal-to-noise ratio may stand in for them.

An alternative the RFC develops in detail is the distance-only approach: if every span is roughly the same length, commonly 80 km, and the fibre has low enough PMD, the only binding constraint is a maximum path distance. Each link then advertises just its length, counted with any transparent network elements converted to an equivalent length of fibre by their loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Two effects dominate. PMD smears pulses depending on polarisation, and it bites hardest at high speeds: on older fibre, 40 Gb/s signals reach only 25 km. Amplifier noise builds up along the way, so a path with error correction can cross about ten amplifier spans, and only three without it. The RFC shows routing can get by with one summed number per link for each effect, or with nothing but path length if the network is built uniformly.

sections.title: What the Control Plane Would Need
sections.content:
The RFC lays out three strategies for distributed routing, and the state each one needs. An operator can pre-qualify paths: check every feasible end-to-end path through a transparent domain for each bit rate in advance, store them in a table, and let routing consult the table. This can work for small sparse networks but may not scale where feasible paths are very many.

Without pre-qualification, routing needs extra per-link state for every impairment that can limit some route: link-PMD-square, link-noise, link-span-length, link-crosstalk or the number of OADM/OXC nodes on the link, and the number of narrow filters. With the distance-only approach the state is just link-distance. Alongside the link values, the bounds must be known: the PMD tolerance parameter, launch power and minimum acceptable ratio for noise, and maximum span length, crosstalk, node count and filter count, all bit-rate dependent.

The RFC notes these physical parameters change slowly and could sit in a database, but today they are often not known at the needed granularity, and if the ingress node does path selection they must be available there. The set of constraints will change as technology evolves, so the control plane should stay open to new parameters.

Wavelength continuity adds a further problem in networks without wavelength conversion: the chosen wavelength must be free on every link of the route. Advertising the state of every wavelength on every link scales poorly, growing with links squared, wavelength count, and change frequency. Probing candidate paths for free wavelengths is one alternative; choosing route and wavelength together, rather than route first, works much better in large mesh networks, at the cost of significant changes to link-state routing such as OSPF.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three levels of ambition: pre-check paths offline and only look them up at routing time, advertise one number per link such as distance or noise, or advertise everything and compute in real time. Whichever level is chosen, the numbers behind the limits must be known somewhere the routing process can reach, and a wavelength must be found free on every link of the path.

sections.title: Networks of All-Optical Islands
sections.content:
Mixing uncoordinated vendors' equipment inside one transparent domain is out of scope. What is realistic is a network of several transparent islands, each optically isolated from the others by transponders that convert to electrical and back, alongside opaque cross-connected regions. The regeneration at each island boundary cleans up the impairments accumulated inside the previous island, but each island may impose its own impairment bounds.

Routing in such a network must know where the islands are, must respect each island's constraints and connectivity limits, and must be sensitive to the cost of hopping between islands. The RFC stresses that one routing decision commits serious money: the equipment for a single coast-to-coast OC-192 link can cost on the order of a million dollars, and circuits are held for months, so hop counts alone will not do as a cost metric. An ultra-long-haul island is likely to be expensive for short hops and economical for long ones, so carriers will expect routing to use it as an express backbone and route circuitously where that pays.

Three distributed approaches look worth investigating: advertise every island's internal topology and constraints globally and let the ingress node compute a strict end-to-end route; have each island advertise only the connectivity, costs and supported rates between its boundary nodes, leaving routing and wavelength selection inside the island; or have the ingress node probe gateway nodes or a management system for guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: Real networks will be a patchwork of transparent islands separated by electrical regeneration. Routing needs to know where the islands are, what each one allows, and what crossing one costs, because a single optical circuit can tie up equipment worth a million dollars for months.

sections.title: Diversity and Shared Risk Link Groups
sections.content:
Two lightpaths are diverse when no single point of failure can take both down, classically a fibre cut. Traditionally data-network operators bought diversity from their private-line providers; GMPLS pulls it into the common control plane, where everyone sees it.

Checking diversity means modelling the physical plant, not just the topology. Fibre cables run in conduits or rights-of-way, often shared by several carriers, sometimes leased from railroads or pipeline companies. Two cables on one route can share a bottleneck such as a tunnel or bridge; cables can cross without a manhole; a splice point can tie a small office's fibres to a major route. Ultra-long systems can interact repeatedly along a route, sharing a right-of-way in one state and crossing in another.

The RFC also argues that simple pairwise diversity is not enough. Customers derive diversity needs from availability targets: a node with lightpaths to two other nodes needs those two paths diverse; an N-lightpath network may describe its needs as an N-by-N matrix. Threats differ too: office fires and floods, shared protected rings, regional disasters. Some networks accept compromises, such as two cables in the same heavy concrete conduit, when the joint failure chance is low enough. The routing algorithm should therefore be sensitive to what the requester counts as unacceptable.

The Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) names the relationship between non-diverse links. The RFC proposes characterising each SRLG by two parameters: the type of compromise, such as shared fibre cable, conduit, right-of-way, optical ring or office without power diversity, and its extent, such as the length of shared plant. Constraints on long, circuitous routes from the impairment rules can make diverse paths harder to find in all-optical networks than in opaque ones. SRLG mappings are defined by operators, cannot yet be self-discovered, and change rarely, so they can live in a central database or be advertised at topology discovery; AT&T experience cited in the RFC has links belonging to over 100 SRLGs each.

On security, the RFC assumes electrical-optical-electrical interfaces at the domain edges; relaxing that would let signals at wrong wavelengths or power levels into the domain. Diversity only helps against physical attack if spare capacity exists to restore the network, SRLGs must be defined so every link vulnerable to an in-scope threat sits in one group, and responsibility for responding to layer-one failures must be allocated between the optical and IP layers to avoid churn. The impairment and SRLG data itself must be protected when stored and when distributed. Control-plane security is out of scope and covered by the GMPLS architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Backup routes must not share failure points, and the real failure points are physical: the same ditch, the same bridge, the same office. The RFC groups links that fail together into shared risk link groups, described by what is shared and for how long, and says routing must treat those groups as first-class information, kept in a database because the equipment cannot discover them alone.
